title: TA505
summary: TA505 is a prolific financially motivated cluster that public reporting has followed since about 2014, known for very high volume email campaigns and for changing its malware families and delivery methods every few months. Vendors have described periods built on downloaders and banking trojans, later periods on the Dridex and Trick families, and periods dominated by the Clop ransomware operation, with victims concentrated in finance, retail, healthcare and education worldwide. The group's defining trait is not a single tool but the speed of change: lures, payloads and infrastructure rotate so quickly that static indicators age within days, while the underlying pattern of invoice and document themed messages stays constant. Defenders should therefore build detections around behaviour and mail flow rather than around specific file hashes, and should test recovery plans for file locking attacks rather than assuming backups are sufficient.

beginner.definition: TA505 is a name for a large criminal group that sends harmful email on a huge scale. Public reports have followed it since around 2014. It often changes the harmful programs it uses, so old warnings quickly become useless. In some years it focused on software that locks files and demands payment. Security companies use names like Hive0065 and Spamdex Tempest for parts of the same activity.
beginner.whyItMatters: Because the tools change often, blocking one program does not stop the group. The next campaign may use a completely different file. What stays the same is the message style: fake invoices, receipts and shipping notes. Training staff to question unexpected attachments works better than memorising file names. Testing your backups also matters, because file locking attacks can spread through a whole company in hours.
howItWorks: The attackers send large numbers of emails with fake invoices or shipping notices.
A link or an attachment downloads a small program that fetches more files for it.
The installed program then steals passwords or gathers more details about the network.
The attackers then choose the next step, such as locking files to demand payment.
They then change the files and the addresses for the next wave of email.
They then reuse whatever worked well, so the pattern repeats with new tools.
beginner.example: Think of a burglar who changes his coat, his car and his accent every month, but always knocks on doors pretending to read the electricity meter. Residents who memorise his old coat are fooled. Residents who check identification every single time are not. The disguise changes; the story does not.
takeaways: Blocking a specific harmful file rarely stops a group that changes tools often.
Write detection rules around behaviour, such as documents that launch scripts.
Test your backup restore process, because file locking spreads quickly.

objectives: Explain why high volume email campaigns are effective despite poor targeting.
Describe why indicator based defences age quickly against a changing group.
Explain how a downloader supports swapping the final payload.
Outline the steps of a file locking incident and the role of tested backups.
Explain why behaviour based detection rules last longer than file hashes.
